SRINAGAR, Indian-controlled Kashmir (CNN) -- India's military on Wednesday accused Pakistani forces of another cease-fire breach in Kashmir. Indian troops in Kashmir go through their drills. This week has seen tensions mount in the region. "Pakistani troops fired six 82-mm mortar rounds in a span of one hour... at our positions," Indian defense spokesman Lt. Col. A. K. Mathur said Wednesday. But the report was denied by Pakistan's army spokesman, Maj. Gen. Athar Abbas, who said there had been no "exchange of fire from our side ... of the LoC [Line of Control]," that divides the Kashmir region between India and Pakistan . Mathur said no Indian forces were wounded in the incident, and they "maintained restraint and didn't retaliate." "We contacted the Pakistan army on the hotline and told them to stop the firing so that the situation doesn't escalate," the Indian spokesman said. But Abbas said he had no reports from local commanders of any incident . "This has been their [India's] allegation but as far as the local commanders are concerned ... there is no incident from our side of any kind," Abbas said. The reported incident came after Monday's border clash in Kashmir, the first major skirmish between South Asia's nuclear rivals since a 2003 cease-fire. India maintains that Pakistani crossed the LoC and fired on Indian soldiers, prompting a firefight. Pakistan blamed India for sparking the incident by crossing into its territory in Kashmir. Senior Pakistani and Indian military officials met briefly Tuesday to discuss the incident, in which one Indian soldier was killed. Pakistan denied reports that its forces sustained casualties. Indian and Pakistani forces have exchanged periodic gunfire since May, but Monday's clashes appear to be a serious setback to the ongoing peace process between the two nations. Indian Defense Minister A. K. Antony blames Pakistan for 19 cease-fire violations since January, which Pakistan denies. Kashmir has been at the root of two wars between India and Pakistan, both of which tested nuclear weapons in 1998. An 18-year separatist campaign in the Indian-controlled portion of the largely Muslim territory has claimed more than 43,000 lives, according to government officials, although human rights groups and non-governmental organizations put the toll at twice that number. India has long accused Pakistan of supporting the separatists in Kashmir, a charge Pakistan denies. India blamed militants from Pakistan for a suicide car bombing outside its embassy in Afghanistan that killed 58 people on July 7. CNN's Mukhtar Ahmad in Srinagar contributed to this report.

**India-Pakistan Tensions Rise in Kashmir After Alleged Cease-Fire Breaches**

*By Staff Reporter*

**SRINAGAR/MUZAFFARABAD —** Tensions between India and Pakistan have risen along the Line of Control in Kashmir after both sides accused each other of violating a cease-fire agreement that has long been viewed as essential to preventing wider conflict between the nuclear-armed neighbors.

Military spokesmen from India and Pakistan issued competing statements alleging that the other side had opened fire across the heavily militarized frontier, which divides the disputed Himalayan region into Indian- and Pakistani-administered areas. Each side said its forces had responded appropriately, while blaming the other for endangering civilians and destabilizing the fragile calm along the border.

Indian officials said Pakistani troops had engaged in “unprovoked firing” in violation of existing understandings, while Pakistan’s military accused Indian forces of initiating the exchange and targeting areas near civilian settlements. Independent verification of the claims was not immediately possible, as access to much of the Line of Control remains restricted.

The latest allegations have renewed concern over the durability of the 2003 cease-fire agreement, which significantly reduced cross-border shelling after years of intense exchanges that killed civilians, displaced border communities and raised fears of escalation. Although the truce has been breached at various points over the past two decades, it has remained a key mechanism for limiting violence along one of the world’s most sensitive military frontiers.

Kashmir has been at the center of India-Pakistan rivalry since the two countries gained independence from Britain in 1947. Both claim the region in full but control separate parts of it. The dispute has sparked multiple wars and repeated crises, including periods of cross-border shelling, militant attacks, and military mobilizations.

India accuses Pakistan of supporting armed groups operating in Indian-administered Kashmir, a charge Islamabad denies. Pakistan says it provides diplomatic and political support to Kashmiris seeking self-determination and accuses India of human rights abuses in the region. New Delhi rejects those allegations and says Kashmir is an integral part of India.

The situation became even more sensitive after India revoked the special constitutional status of Jammu and Kashmir in 2019, a move Pakistan condemned and which led to a further deterioration in diplomatic ties. In 2021, the two militaries reaffirmed their commitment to the 2003 cease-fire, leading to a significant reduction in violence along the Line of Control.

Residents in border areas have often borne the brunt of flare-ups. Schools, homes and farms near the frontier have repeatedly been affected during previous exchanges of fire, forcing families to seek shelter or relocate temporarily. Local officials on both sides have warned that renewed hostilities could again disrupt civilian life.

Analysts say the immediate risk of a broader conflict depends on whether the latest incident remains isolated or becomes part of a wider pattern of retaliation. They note that communication channels between the two militaries, including hotlines and flag meetings, have in the past helped prevent localized clashes from escalating.

Diplomatic relations between India and Pakistan remain largely frozen, with limited formal dialogue and continuing disputes over terrorism, territorial claims and political rights in Kashmir. International actors have frequently urged both countries to exercise restraint, though India has traditionally opposed third-party mediation, insisting that Kashmir-related issues be addressed bilaterally.

For now, the latest accusations underscore the fragility of peace along the Line of Control and the persistent volatility of the Kashmir dispute. While the 2003 cease-fire remains an important stabilizing arrangement, renewed allegations of breaches show how quickly tensions can resurface in a conflict that has remained unresolved for more than seven decades.
